You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Living creature

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In Christian teaching, 'living creature' (Hebrew chayyah/chayyot; Greek zōon/zōa) most commonly refers to the four living creatures of the divine throne visions, understood as an exalted order of angelic beings — identified with the cherubim — who attend God's throne and lead the worship of heaven. Symbolically, they are most often taken to represent the whole of animate creation (wild beasts, domestic animals, humanity, and birds, via the lion, ox, man, and eagle faces) gathered in ceaseless praise before God, testifying to God's sovereignty over all living things.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Ezekiel 1:5-14 (the four living creatures in the chariot-throne vision)",
    "Ezekiel 10:14-22 (the living creatures explicitly identified as cherubim)",
    "Revelation 4:6-9 (four living creatures around the throne, full of eyes, crying 'Holy, holy, holy')",
    "Revelation 5:8-14; 6:1-8; 7:11; 19:4 (the living creatures in heavenly worship and judgment scenes)",
    "Isaiah 6:1-3 (the seraphim, frequently cited as a parallel throne-attendant order)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "The four living creatures as symbols of the four Evangelists/Gospels (traditionally: Matthew–man, Mark–lion, Luke–ox, John–eagle), a reading rooted in Irenaeus, Jerome, and Augustine and pervasive in Christian art and liturgy.",
      "basis": [
        "Revelation 4:6-8",
        "Ezekiel 1:10",
        "Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.11.8; Jerome, preface to his Matthew commentary; Augustine, De Consensu Evangelistarum 1.6"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The living creatures as emblems of divine attributes or of aspects of Christ (majesty/royalty in the lion, strength/service in the ox, intelligence/wisdom in the man, swiftness/heavenly vision in the eagle).",
      "basis": [
        "Ezekiel 1:10",
        "Revelation 4:7",
        "patristic and medieval homiletic tradition (e.g., Gregory the Great)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The four faces correspond to the standards of the four lead tribes in Israel's wilderness camp (Judah–lion, Ephraim–ox, Reuben–man, Dan–eagle), so the creatures symbolize God enthroned amid His covenant people.",
      "basis": [
        "Numbers 2 (camp arrangement)",
        "rabbinic tradition applied to Ezekiel 1 and Revelation 4"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "A cosmological/astral reading: the four creatures reflect the four cardinal points or the four fixed zodiacal signs (Leo, Taurus, Aquarius/man, Scorpio-eagle), symbolizing God's dominion over the ordered cosmos; found in some history-of-religions scholarship.",
      "basis": [
        "Ezekiel 1",
        "Revelation 4:6-8",
        "ancient Near Eastern iconographic parallels cited in critical scholarship"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The non-symbolic lexical sense: in Genesis, 'living creature' (nephesh chayyah) simply denotes any animate being — animals and, in Genesis 2:7, the human as a 'living soul/being' — used in theological anthropology (humans and animals share creaturely life) rather than as a symbol.",
      "basis": [
        "Genesis 1:20-24",
        "Genesis 2:7, 2:19",
        "Genesis 9:10-16 (covenant with every living creature)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is broad, recognizable consensus that the 'living creatures' of Ezekiel and Revelation are cherubim-class angelic throne attendants, since Ezekiel 10 makes the identification explicit; that identification is essentially settled. What varies is the further symbolic significance assigned to them: representation of all creation is the most common scholarly and devotional reading, while the four-Evangelists association is the most historically influential ecclesial reading (dominant in art and lectionary symbolism, though most modern exegetes treat it as later typology rather than the text's original sense). If the author's term instead targets the Genesis usage (nephesh chayyah), the consensus there is lexical rather than symbolic: 'living creature/being' denotes animate life generally, and claims of a distinct symbolic meaning in that context would not reflect settled interpretation."
}

{

      "basis": [

      "prominence": "dominant"

  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is broad agreement that the visionary living creatures of Ezekiel and Revelation are heavenly throne attendants, with Ezekiel explicitly calling them cherubim. There is no settled consensus on one further symbolic referent. Representation of the whole created order and identification with the four Evangelists are both major Christian interpretations, while the latter is especially prominent in historic Christian art and tradition. Context is decisive because the phrase elsewhere can be a nonsymbolic designation for living beings."

No major competing symbolic system has displaced these."

BOOK ENTRY
A nation — as the beasts of Daniel's sea are kingdoms, the living creatures in Revelation's sea are peoples.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
(none)

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Dan 7:3, 17; Rev 8:9; 16:3) · see The Bow, ch. 44

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Daniel 7:3 — And four great beasts came up from the sea, diverse one from another.
Daniel 7:17 — These great beasts, which are four, are four kings, which shall arise out of the earth.
Revelation 8:9 — And the third part of the creatures which were in the sea, and had life, died; and the third part of the ships were destroyed.
Revelation 16:3 — And the second angel poured out his vial upon the sea; and it became as the blood of a dead man: and every living soul died in the sea.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
